items.en: Body, Breath, and Mind: Abiding in and Emerging from Meditation
items.zh: 調身息心 · 住 · 出

zh: 第二、住坐中調三事者。當一坐之中，隨時長短，攝念用心。是中應善識身、息、心三事調不調相。若坐時，上雖調身意而令身或寬或急，或偏或曲，低昂不俱。覺已隨正，每令安隱，中無寬急，平直正住。復次，當坐之中，身雖調和，而氣或不調。不調相者，如上所說，或風喘，或氣急，身中脹滿。當用前法隨治之，每令息道綿綿，如有如無。復次，一坐時中，身息雖調，而心或沈或浮，寬急不俱。爾時若覺，當用前法調令中適。此三事的無前後，隨不調者而調適之，令一坐之中，身、息、心三事調適，無相乖越，和融不二，此則能除宿患，障妨不生，定道可剋。
en: Second, harmonizing the three things while abiding in sitting meditation. Throughout the course of a single sitting, however long or short it may last, the mind should be gathered and applied with continuous care. Here, one should skillfully recognize the harmonized and unharmonized marks of the three things — body, breath, and mind.

While sitting, even if the body was properly harmonized at the outset, it may come to be too slack or too tense, tilted or bent, uneven in its posture — once this is noticed, it should be corrected at once, always kept comfortable and secure, neither slack nor tense throughout, level and upright.

Furthermore, throughout the sitting, even if the body remains harmonized, the breath may become unharmonized — its unharmonized marks are as described above: wind or panting, or breath-with-effort, with the body feeling swollen and full. This should be remedied at once using the methods already given, always keeping the breath's path continuous and fine, as though present and yet almost imperceptible.

Furthermore, throughout a single sitting, even if body and breath remain harmonized, the mind may come to sink or float, become too slack or too tense. If this is noticed at such a time, it should be adjusted back to its proper measure using the methods already given.

These three things have no fixed order among them — whichever becomes unharmonized should be adjusted accordingly, so that, throughout the course of a single sitting, body, breath, and mind remain harmonized together, without contradiction, blended and undivided. In this way, longstanding troubles can be removed, no obstacle or difficulty arises, and the achievement of concentration can be attained.

zh:
第三、若坐禪將竟，欲出定時，應前放心異緣，開口放氣，想息從百脈隨意而散，然後微微動身，次動肩胛及頭頸，次動兩足，悉令柔軟，然後以手遍摩諸毛孔，次摩手令暖，以掩兩眼，却手，然後開目，待身熱汗稍歇，方可隨意出入。若不爾者，或得住心，出既斗促，則細法未散，住在身中，令人頭痛，百骨節強，猶如風勞，於後坐中，煩躁不安，是故心不欲坐。每須在意，此為出定調身、息、心方法。以從細出麁故，是名善入出住。如偈說：
進止有次第，麁細不相違，
譬如善調馬，欲去而欲住。
en:
Third, when sitting meditation is about to conclude and one wishes to emerge from concentration, one should first release the mind toward other objects, open the mouth and release the breath, imagining it dispersing at will through the hundred channels of the body; then gently move the body, next the shoulders, head, and neck, then the two feet, making all of them supple; then use the hands to massage every pore of the skin, next rub the hands until they are warm and cover the two eyes with them, then withdraw the hands and open the eyes, waiting until the body's warmth and perspiration have gradually subsided before moving and resting freely as one wishes. If this is not done — if, for instance, the mind was in the midst of settled concentration and one emerges too abruptly — the subtle qualities of that state will not yet have dispersed and will remain lodged within the body, causing headaches and stiffness throughout the hundred joints, much like a rheumatic disorder, resulting in restlessness and unease in later sittings, so that the mind becomes reluctant to sit at all. This point must always be kept in mind — this is the method for harmonizing body, breath, and mind upon emerging from concentration, moving from the fine back out into the coarse. This is what is meant by skillfully entering, abiding in, and emerging from concentration. As the verse says:
"Advancing and resting each have their own proper sequence, the coarse and the fine never at odds with one another —
Just as with a well-trained horse, whether it is made to go or made to stay."

The warning about emerging from meditation too abruptly — headaches, joint stiffness, a rheumatic-like malaise, and a resulting reluctance ever to sit again — is notably specific and clinical for a text this old, and matches lived experience reported across many later meditation traditions: how a session ends matters nearly as much as how it begins. This closes 調五法 (harmonizing the five things), the fourth of the twenty-five preliminary conditions' five groups, and the treatise's fullest practical instruction so far.

intro: The fifth and final group of the twenty-five preliminary conditions closes the external expedient means — five qualities of mind a practitioner actively cultivates, rather than external circumstances arranged or internal obstacles removed.

zh: 第五、行五法者：一、欲；二、精進；三、念；四、巧慧；五、一心。欲者，行人初修禪時，欲從欲界中出，欲得初禪，故亦名為志，亦名為願，亦名為樂，是人內心志願好樂諸禪定故。問曰：悕望心生，於修禪中則為妨礙，云何以此為方便耶？答曰：夫欲者，秖是大志成就願樂之心，故名為欲，不應於用心時起悕望憶想之念。若悕望心起，則不澄靜；若心不澄靜，則諸三昧無由得發矣。
en: Fifth, practicing the five dharmas: first, aspiration; second, diligence; third, mindfulness; fourth, skillful wisdom; fifth, one-pointedness of mind.

Aspiration: when a practitioner first cultivates dhyāna, wishing to emerge from the desire realm and attain the first dhyāna, this is also called resolve, also called vow, also called delight — since the practitioner's inner mind is resolved upon and delights in the various dhyānas. Question: If a mind of longing and expectation arises, does this not become an obstacle to cultivating dhyāna — how, then, can this be taken as an expedient means? Answer: "Aspiration" here means simply the mind of great resolve accomplishing its vowed delight — hence it is called aspiration; it does not mean that, while actually applying the mind in practice, one should give rise to thoughts of longing and expectant recollection. If a mind of longing and expectation arises, the mind will not be clear and still; and if the mind is not clear and still, no samādhi whatsoever can ever be brought forth.

zh: 二、精進者，有二種：一、身精進；二、心精進。行者若能修十二頭陀，即是具足身心精進。如佛告迦葉：「阿蘭若比丘，遠離二著，形心清淨，行頭陀。頭陀者，有十二事：一、阿蘭若處；二、常行乞食；三、次第乞食；四、受一食法；五、節量食；六、中後不飲漿；七、著弊衣；八、但三衣；九、塚間住；十、樹下止；十一、露地坐；十二、常坐不臥。是名十二頭陀。」如《頭陀經》中所明，是中應廣說。頭陀者，名抖擻，抖擻身心諸不善法故。若修禪時，行此等法，是名不放逸行，具足身心精進。當知此人能得三乘聖果，何況世間禪定。復次，行者為修禪故，持戒清淨，棄捨五蓋，初夜、後夜專精不廢，譬如鑽火未然，終不休息，是名精進。如佛告阿難：「諸佛一心勤精進，故得三菩提。」何況餘善道法？
en: Second, diligence: this is of two kinds — bodily diligence and mental diligence. If a practitioner is able to cultivate the twelve dhutanga practices, this is precisely being complete in both bodily and mental diligence. As the Buddha told Kāśyapa: "A forest-dwelling monk, far removed from the two kinds of attachment, pure in body and mind, practices the dhutanga austerities. The dhutanga practices are twelve in number: first, dwelling in a forest hermitage; second, constantly practicing alms-begging; third, begging for alms in sequence without discrimination; fourth, receiving only a single meal a day; fifth, eating with moderation; sixth, not drinking juice after midday; seventh, wearing discarded, worn-out robes; eighth, keeping only the three robes; ninth, dwelling among graves; tenth, resting beneath trees; eleventh, sitting in the open air; twelfth, constantly sitting and never lying down. These are called the twelve dhutanga practices." This is explained in full in the Dhutanga Sūtra, and should be given in full detail there.

"Dhutanga" means "shaking off" — shaking off every unwholesome dharma of body and mind. If, while cultivating dhyāna, one practices these methods, this is called conduct free of laxity, complete in both bodily and mental diligence. One should know that such a person is able to attain the noble fruits of all three vehicles — how much more so the dhyāna of the ordinary world?

Furthermore, a practitioner who, for the sake of cultivating dhyāna, upholds the precepts purely, abandons the five hindrances, and applies undivided effort without neglect through the first and last watches of the night — like drilling for fire without ever pausing until the fire catches — this is called diligence. As the Buddha told Ānanda: "Every buddha, with a single-pointed mind, diligently applies effort, and therefore attains saṃbodhi, perfect awakening." How much more so, then, every other wholesome path?

zh: 三、念者，如《摩訶衍》中說：「念欲界不淨，欺誑可賤，念初禪為尊重可貴。」此與六行意同，但立名異。六行觀者：一、厭下苦、麁、障為三，即是觀欲不淨，欺誑可賤；攀上勝、妙、出為三，即是觀初禪為尊重可貴。今釋六法，自可為二意：一、約果明；二約因明。先約欲界果明，言「厭下苦、麁、障」者，厭患欲界底下色心麁重故。行者思惟：今感欲界報身，饑渴、寒熱、病痛、刀杖等種種所逼，故名苦。麁者，此身為三十六物屎尿臭穢之所成，故名為麁。麁者，醜陋故。障者，此身質礙，不得自在，為山河石壁所隔礙，故名為障。次約色界果明「攀上勝」者，行者思惟，知色界樂為上勝故。如欲界樂為苦，色界樂為勝，得樂勝苦，故名上勝。「妙」者，受得色界之身，如鏡中像，雖有形色，無有質礙，故名為妙。「出」者，獲得五通，徹見障外等事，山壁無礙，故名為出。二、明因中六行者，先約欲界因，明厭下苦、麁、障者。行者思惟：若於報身中所起心數緣於貪欲，不能出離，如經說「一切眾生為愛奴僕」，故名為苦。麁者，緣欲界五塵散動起惡，故名為麁。障者，為煩惱蓋覆，故名為障。次約色界因，明攀上勝、妙、出者。行者思惟：初禪上勝之樂從樂內發，故名為上勝。貪欲樂從外五塵生，惱熱怨結，以為下劣，不如妙者禪定之樂，心定不動，而樂法成就，故名為妙。貪欲之樂，心亂馳動，故名為麁。出者，心得出離蓋障，至初禪，故名為出，亦如石泉不從外來，內自涌出。今因此六行釋於念義，意在可見。問曰：今說佛弟子修禪，何用說凡夫六行觀法？答曰：既說三界共禪，亦應知其所行之因。若佛弟子用八聖種，起十六行觀，離欲為念，入初禪，則無過失。在下明無漏禪中當廣分別。
en: Third, mindfulness: as the Mahāyāna treatise says: "Be mindful that the desire realm is impure, deceptive, and contemptible; be mindful that the first dhyāna is to be honored and cherished." This shares the same sense as the six contemplations, differing only in name. The six contemplations are: growing weary of the lower realm's suffering, coarseness, and obstruction — three in number, which is precisely contemplating desire as impure, deceptive, and contemptible; and reaching for the superiority, subtlety, and transcendence of the higher realm — three more, which is precisely contemplating the first dhyāna as honorable and cherished.

Now, in explaining these six items, there are, in themselves, two aspects: explained in terms of the fruit, and explained in terms of the cause. First, explained in terms of the fruit within the desire realm: as for "growing weary of the lower realm's suffering, coarseness, and obstruction" — this means growing weary of the coarse, heavy body and mind of the lower desire realm. The practitioner reflects: the retributive body received within the desire realm now is pressed upon by hunger and thirst, cold and heat, sickness and pain, blade and rod, and every other kind of affliction — hence it is called suffering. "Coarseness" means that this body is made up of the thirty-six foul, unclean things such as excrement and urine — hence it is called coarse, coarse because it is ugly and repulsive. "Obstruction" means that this body, being made of solid matter, cannot move freely, blocked and hindered by mountains, rivers, and stone walls — hence it is called obstruction.

Next, explained in terms of the fruit within the form realm: as for "reaching for what is superior" — the practitioner reflects and comes to know that the bliss of the form realm is superior. Just as the bliss of the desire realm is suffering, the bliss of the form realm is superior — attaining bliss that surpasses suffering, and so it is called superior. As for "subtlety" — the body received in the form realm is like a reflection in a mirror: though it has form and color, it possesses no material obstruction, and so it is called subtle. As for "transcendence" — attaining the five supernormal powers, one sees clearly through obstructions to what lies beyond, unhindered by mountains and walls, and so it is called transcendence.

Second, clarifying the six contemplations in terms of the cause: first, in terms of the cause within the desire realm, clarifying "growing weary of suffering, coarseness, and obstruction." The practitioner reflects: if, within this retributive body, the mental factors that arise take craving desire as their object and one cannot escape it, then, as the sūtra says, "all sentient beings are slaves to craving" — hence it is called suffering. "Coarseness" means that, taking the five defiling objects of the desire realm as its object, the mind stirs and scatters, giving rise to unwholesome deeds — hence it is called coarse. "Obstruction" means being covered over by the hindrance of affliction — hence it is called obstruction. Next, in terms of the cause within the form realm, clarifying "reaching for what is superior, subtle, and transcendent." The practitioner reflects: the superior bliss of the first dhyāna arises from within the bliss itself — hence it is called superior. The bliss of craving desire arises from the five external defiling objects, bound up with vexation and heat and enmity, and is thus inferior; it is not like the subtle bliss of dhyāna-concentration, in which the mind is settled and unmoving while the dharma of bliss is accomplished — hence it is called subtle. The bliss of craving desire, by contrast, leaves the mind scattered and racing about — hence it is called coarse. "Transcendence" means that the mind attains freedom from the covering hindrances and reaches the first dhyāna — hence it is called transcendence, just as a spring welling up from rock does not come from outside but wells up of itself from within.

This, then, explains the meaning of mindfulness in terms of these six contemplations — the intent should now be clear. Question: Since this passage is describing how a disciple of the Buddha cultivates dhyāna, what use is there in explaining the six contemplations practiced by ordinary, unenlightened people? Answer: Since it has already been said that dhyāna is shared in common across the three realms, one should also know the causes behind whatever is practiced there. If a disciple of the Buddha makes use of the eight noble lineages, gives rise to the sixteen aspects of contemplation, and takes freedom from desire as the object of mindfulness in order to enter the first dhyāna, then there is no fault in this at all. This will be distinguished fully further below, where the uncontaminated dhyānas are clarified.

zh: 四、巧慧者，籌量欲界樂、初禪樂得失輕重之相。今翻覆作二釋：言籌量者，即是用智慧思度之名。得失者，欲界樂為失，初禪樂為得。初禪樂無過失，故為得；欲界樂過失，故名為失。亦可言初禪為失，欲界樂為得者，欲界樂麁故，計以為實，生重得心；初禪為失者，覺身空寂，受於細樂，似若無故，不可定取，失樂相貌，故名為失。言輕重者，欲界為輕，初禪為重。欲界輕者，五識相應所得樂迅速，淺故為輕；初禪所得樂重，意識相應久住，緣深故名重。重者，可貴寶重。亦得言欲界為重，初禪為輕者，欲界樂與煩惱俱心累重故，故名重；初禪樂心累少，故名為輕。次有師言巧慧者，行人初修禪時，善識內外方便，巧而用之，不失其宜，疾得禪定，故名巧慧也。五、一心者，行人已善能巧慧籌量，用心無謬，今但應專心守一而行，故名一心。如人欲行善，須識道路通塞之相，決定知已，即一心而去，故說非智不禪，非禪不智，義在此也。
en: Fourth, skillful wisdom: weighing the marks of gain and loss, light and heavy, between the bliss of the desire realm and the bliss of the first dhyāna. Here two explanations are given, turned over from opposite sides. As to "weighing": this is simply the name for using wisdom to deliberate and measure. As to "gain and loss": the bliss of the desire realm is a loss, and the bliss of the first dhyāna is a gain — since the bliss of the first dhyāna has no fault, it is called a gain, and since the bliss of the desire realm has fault, it is called a loss. It may also be said, conversely, that the first dhyāna is a loss and the bliss of the desire realm is a gain: because the bliss of the desire realm is coarse, it is taken to be real, and gives rise to a strong sense of gain; the first dhyāna, by contrast, is felt as loss because the body is perceived as empty and still, experiencing a subtle bliss that seems almost like nothing at all, unable to be fixed and grasped — losing, in this way, the very appearance of bliss, and so it is called a loss.

As to "light and heavy": the desire realm is light, and the first dhyāna is heavy. The desire realm is light because the bliss obtained there, associated with the five sense-consciousnesses, is swift and shallow. The bliss obtained in the first dhyāna is heavy because it is associated with the mind-consciousness, abides for a long time, and takes a deep object — hence it is called heavy, "heavy" here meaning precious and weighty. It may also be said, conversely, that the desire realm is heavy and the first dhyāna is light: the bliss of the desire realm is heavy because it comes bound up together with affliction, weighing down the mind; the bliss of the first dhyāna is light because the mind is only lightly encumbered. Next, some masters say that skillful wisdom means this: when a practitioner first cultivates dhyāna, they skillfully recognize the internal and external expedient means and apply them with skill, never losing what is proper to the moment, and thereby swiftly attain dhyāna-concentration — hence this too is called skillful wisdom.

Fifth, one-pointedness of mind: once a practitioner is already able to skillfully weigh matters through wisdom, applying the mind without error, they should now simply devote the mind single-mindedly, holding to the one and proceeding accordingly — hence this is called one-pointedness of mind. It is like a person wishing to travel, who must first know well which roads are open and which are blocked, and, having determined this with certainty, then proceeds with a single, undivided mind. Hence it is said: "without wisdom, there is no dhyāna; without dhyāna, there is no wisdom" — the meaning lies exactly here.

zh: 釋禪波羅蜜次第法門卷第二
en: End of Fascicle Two of the Shi Chan Boluomi Cidi Famen.

The "six contemplations" under mindfulness are a repurposed piece of Abhidharma technical apparatus (the standard method for progressing between any two meditative levels), applied here specifically to the move out of the desire realm into the first dhyāna — worth noting is Zhiyi's own aside defending why a treatise for Buddhist disciples bothers explaining a scheme originally used by "ordinary, unenlightened people": because dhyāna itself, as topic 4 already established, is shared in common across every kind of practitioner, only the causes behind the practice differ. "Skillful wisdom" and "one-pointedness" then close the five practiced dharmas by turning outward analysis fully inward — weighing gain against loss, then simply committing to the path once weighed. This closes 行五法 (practicing the five dharmas), the fifth and final group of the twenty-five preliminary conditions, and with it the external expedient means and fascicle 2 as a whole. Topic 6 itself continues: as the interlinear note at the head of this fascicle says, it runs across three fascicles, and fascicle 3 turns to the internal expedient means.

quiz.q: How does the text describe the direction of entering and of emerging from concentration?
options: entering moves from coarse to fine (body, breath, mind); emerging moves from fine to coarse
quiz.why: "When one wishes to enter concentration, the movement is, by its very nature, from the coarse into the fine: the body, being coarsest, comes first; the breath, situated between, comes next; the mind, being finest of all, comes last." Emerging is described as "moving from the fine back out into the coarse."

quiz.q: What does the text say happens if one emerges from concentration too abruptly?
options: the subtle state does not disperse and lodges in the body, causing headaches and stiff joints like a rheumatic disorder, restlessness in later sittings, and reluctance to sit
all effort lost; the precepts must be retaken
quiz.why: "If the mind was in the midst of settled concentration and one emerges too abruptly — the subtle qualities of that state will not yet have dispersed and will remain lodged within the body, causing headaches and stiffness throughout the hundred joints, much like a rheumatic disorder."

quiz.q: Why is the first of the five practiced dharmas, aspiration, not the obstructing mind of longing?
options: aspiration is the mind of great resolve accomplishing its vowed delight; one should not give rise to longing while actually applying the mind
because aspiration is the hindrance of desire
because it arises only after concentration
quiz.why: "'Aspiration' here means simply the mind of great resolve accomplishing its vowed delight — hence it is called aspiration; it does not mean that, while actually applying the mind in practice, one should give rise to thoughts of longing and expectant recollection. If a mind of longing and expectation arises, the mind will not be clear and still."
